metric-axioms.name: The metric axioms
metric-axioms.oneLine: A metric is any function of two points satisfying four conditions — non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry and the triangle inequality — and everything else about distance is deduced from those and not from the picture.

metric-examples.oneLine: The Euclidean metric is one metric on R^n, not the meaning of distance: the discrete, maximum and taxicab metrics are all genuine metrics and they disagree about which points are close.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

open-balls.name: Open balls
open-balls.oneLine: B(x, r) is every point strictly within r of x, and what it looks like depends on the metric and on the space it is drawn in — the same formula gives a disc, a square, or a single point.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

ambient-space.name: The ambient space
ambient-space.oneLine: Open, closed and ball are never properties of a set alone: they are properties of a set inside a particular space, and the same set changes its answer when the surrounding space does.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

open-sets.name: Open sets
open-sets.oneLine: A set is open when every point of it has a ball around it that stays inside — which makes openness a statement about having room to move, not about the shape of the boundary.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

closed-sets.name: Closed sets
closed-sets.oneLine: Closed means the complement is open, which is not the opposite of open: a set can be both, or neither, and most sets are neither.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

convergence.name: Convergence in a metric space
convergence.oneLine: A sequence converges to x when the distances to x eventually stay below any epsilon you name — so convergence is about the distances, and changes when the metric does.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

limit-uniqueness.name: Limits are unique
limit-uniqueness.oneLine: A sequence in a metric space has at most one limit, and the proof is one line of the triangle inequality — which is also why it fails in spaces that are not metric.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

cauchy-sequences.name: Cauchy sequences
cauchy-sequences.oneLine: A Cauchy sequence is one whose terms get arbitrarily close to each other, which is a condition you can check without knowing the limit — and is strictly weaker than converging.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

completeness.name: Completeness
completeness.oneLine: A space is complete when every Cauchy sequence actually converges in it; completeness is a property of the space, and removing a single point can destroy it.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

continuity-metric.name: Continuity between metric spaces
continuity-metric.oneLine: Continuity has three equivalent faces — epsilon–delta, preimages of open sets being open, and preservation of limits of sequences — and which one to reach for is most of the skill.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

compactness.name: Compactness
compactness.oneLine: Compact means every open cover has a finite subcover; in R^n that is exactly closed and bounded, and in a general metric space it is exactly sequential compactness — but those are theorems, not definitions.

readings.title: Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces (Sutherland)

sample-space.name: Sample spaces and events
sample-space.oneLine: A probability model is a set of outcomes, a collection of events which are subsets of it, and a measure on those — and most mistakes are made before any arithmetic, by writing down the wrong set.

counting.name: Counting
counting.oneLine: When outcomes are equally likely a probability is a ratio of counts, so the work is combinatorial: multiplication, permutations, and binomial coefficients for choices where order does not matter.

conditional-probability.name: Conditional probability
conditional-probability.oneLine: P(A|B) is the probability of A in a world restricted to B, which is why conditioning changes the sample space and not merely the arithmetic.

bayes.name: Bayes' theorem
bayes.oneLine: Bayes turns P(B|A) into P(A|B) by weighting with the prior, and the whole content of it is that those two conditionals are different numbers.

independence.name: Independence
independence.oneLine: Independent means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) — a statement about a product, which has nothing to do with the events being disjoint and is usually the opposite of it.

random-variables.name: Discrete random variables
random-variables.oneLine: A random variable is a function from the sample space to the numbers, and its distribution is what you get when you forget the sample space and keep only the probabilities of its values.

distributions.name: Named discrete distributions
distributions.oneLine: Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and Poisson are not separate topics but four answers to four different questions about repeated trials, and picking the wrong one is picking the wrong question.

expectation.name: Expectation
expectation.oneLine: The expectation is the probability-weighted average of the values, and it is linear whether or not anything is independent — which is the single most useful fact in the subject.

indicator-variables.name: Indicator variables
indicator-variables.oneLine: An indicator is 1 when an event happens and 0 when it does not, so its expectation is the probability of the event — which turns awkward counting problems into sums of easy ones.

variance.name: Variance
variance.oneLine: Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean, computed as E[X^2] - (E[X])^2, and unlike expectation it only adds across independent variables.

joint-distributions.name: Joint distributions
joint-distributions.oneLine: A joint distribution says how two random variables behave together; the marginals are what is left when one is summed away, and they do not determine the joint unless the variables are independent.

continuous-distributions.name: Continuous distributions
continuous-distributions.oneLine: A continuous random variable has a density rather than a probability at each point, so P(X = x) is zero and probabilities come from integrating over an interval.

cache-associativity.name: Associativity and replacement
cache-associativity.oneLine: A set with several ways gives a block more than one place to live, and the moment there is a choice of where to put it there is a choice of what to throw out.

ms-metric-axioms.oneLine: Three conditions — positivity with d(x,y)=0 only when x=y, symmetry, and the triangle inequality — are the whole definition of distance, and everything in the unit is deduced from them and from nothing else.

ms-discrete-metric.name: The discrete metric
ms-discrete-metric.oneLine: Zero between a point and itself and one between any two different points: a metric that keeps all three axioms and throws every geometric intuition away, which is why it is the first place to test a claim you suspect.

ms-subspace-metric.name: Restricting a metric to a subset
ms-subspace-metric.oneLine: Any nonempty subset of a metric space is a metric space under the same distance function, which is how one set can sit inside two different ambient spaces and answer differently in each.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-reverse-triangle.name: The reverse triangle inequality
ms-reverse-triangle.oneLine: Distances to a common point cannot differ by more than the distance between the two places you measured from: |d(x,y) − d(y,z)| ≤ d(x,z), proved by applying the triangle inequality twice and reading it both ways.

ms-euclidean-metrics.name: The three metrics on R^n
ms-euclidean-metrics.oneLine: Summing the coordinate differences, taking their root mean square, or taking the largest of them each gives a metric on R^n; only the second needs Cauchy–Schwarz to get the triangle inequality.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-hamming-distance.name: Hamming distance
ms-hamming-distance.oneLine: On binary strings of a fixed length, counting the positions where two strings differ is a metric — the triangle inequality holds because every disagreement between x and z must show up against any third string.

ms-sequence-spaces.name: The sequence spaces
ms-sequence-spaces.oneLine: The obvious coordinatewise formulas only define metrics once the space is cut down to the sequences they stay finite on — absolutely summable for the sum, square-summable for the root, bounded for the supremum.

ms-normed-spaces.name: Norms, and the metrics they give
ms-normed-spaces.oneLine: A norm measures a single vector; subtracting first turns it into a metric. Not every metric arises this way, and homogeneity is the condition that fails — the discrete metric is the standard witness.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-function-spaces.name: Spaces of functions
ms-function-spaces.oneLine: Bounded functions under the supremum norm, and continuous functions on a closed interval under the same norm or under the integral of the absolute value: the distance between two functions becomes a single number.

ms-matrix-algebras.oneLine: Singular values give several norms on the n-by-n matrices, and therefore several metrics on them. Marked non-examinable in the notes.

ms-path-and-word-metrics.name: Path and word metrics
ms-path-and-word-metrics.oneLine: Distance as the length of the shortest route: along paths in a space, or along generators in a group. Both are marked non-examinable in the notes.

ms-open-balls.oneLine: The set of points strictly within r of a centre. Every later definition is phrased with these, and what one looks like depends on the metric and on the ambient space, not on the formula alone.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-closed-balls-boundedness.name: Closed balls, and bounded sets
ms-closed-balls-boundedness.oneLine: Swapping the strict inequality for a weak one gives the closed ball, and a set is bounded when some single ball contains it — a property of the metric, so the whole of R is bounded under the discrete one.

readings.where: Ch. 6.1, closed balls and bounded sets

ms-convergence.name: Convergence in a metric space
ms-convergence.oneLine: A sequence converges to x when every ball about x eventually contains all of it; equivalently when the real sequence of distances tends to zero. The positivity axiom is exactly what makes the limit unique.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-cauchy-sequences.name: Cauchy sequences
ms-cauchy-sequences.oneLine: Terms that eventually get close to each other rather than to a named limit. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy; the converse is a property of the space, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-continuity.name: Continuity at a point, and sequentially
ms-continuity.oneLine: The epsilon–delta definition carried over with distances in place of absolute values, and the equivalent statement that f takes every sequence converging to a to a sequence converging to f(a).

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-uniform-continuity.name: Uniform continuity
ms-uniform-continuity.oneLine: One delta has to work at every point at once. The quantifier moves, and that is the whole difference: squaring on the whole line and the reciprocal on (0,1) are continuous and not uniformly so.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-uniform-convergence.name: Pointwise against uniform convergence
ms-uniform-convergence.oneLine: Pointwise convergence lets each x choose its own N; uniform convergence is convergence of the suprema, which is convergence in the supremum metric. The moving bump separates them.

ms-uniform-limit-theorems.name: What survives a uniform limit
ms-uniform-limit-theorems.oneLine: Continuity passes to a uniform limit, and so does the integral; the derivative does not, unless it is the derivatives that converge uniformly. Three theorems, and three counterexamples if you drop "uniform".

ms-completeness.name: Complete metric spaces
ms-completeness.oneLine: A space is complete when being Cauchy is enough to converge in it. Completeness is a property of the space, not of the sequence: the same sequence is Cauchy in Q and in R and converges in only one of them.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-adherent-points-closure.name: Adherent points and the closure
ms-adherent-points-closure.oneLine: A point is adherent to E when every ball about it meets E, equivalently when some sequence in E converges to it. The closure is E together with all of them, and it is the smallest closed set containing E.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-closed-sets.name: Closed sets
ms-closed-sets.oneLine: A set is closed when it already contains every point adherent to it — equivalently, when the limit of every convergent sequence of its points lands back inside. Closed balls and finite sets are closed.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-complete-iff-closed.name: Complete subspaces are the closed ones
ms-complete-iff-closed.oneLine: Inside a complete space, a subspace is complete exactly when it is closed. Both directions are short, and together they turn a question about sequences into a question about one set.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-isometries-lipschitz.name: Isometries, Lipschitz maps and contractions
ms-isometries-lipschitz.oneLine: Maps graded by how much they can stretch: exactly one, at most K, and at most K with K strictly below one. Every Lipschitz map is uniformly continuous, and a map can shrink every distance without being a contraction.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-dense-sets.name: Dense subsets
ms-dense-sets.oneLine: E is dense in X when its closure is all of X — every point of X is a limit of points of E. Whether a set is dense depends on the metric: the rationals are dense in R and nowhere near it under the discrete metric.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-completion.name: The completion of a metric space
ms-completion.oneLine: Every metric space sits as a dense subspace of a complete one, and that complete one is essentially unique. It is how R is built from Q, and it is why an incomplete space is never a dead end.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-complete-function-spaces.name: Completeness of the function spaces
ms-complete-function-spaces.oneLine: Bounded functions under the supremum norm form a complete space, and the continuous bounded ones are a closed subspace of it — which is the uniform limit theorem of chapter 2, said as a fact about a space.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-banach-fixed-point.name: Banach’s fixed-point theorem
ms-banach-fixed-point.oneLine: A contraction of a nonempty complete space has exactly one fixed point, and iterating from anywhere finds it. Completeness cannot be dropped, and neither can the uniform contraction constant.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-interior-open-sets.name: Interior points and open sets
ms-interior-open-sets.oneLine: A point is interior to E when some ball about it stays inside E, and E is open when all of its points are. Open balls are open — which has to be proved, and the proof is the triangle inequality.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-open-set-algebra.name: How open and closed sets combine
ms-open-set-algebra.oneLine: Any union and any finite intersection of open sets is open; complements swap open for closed, so closed sets take any intersection and finite unions. The word "finite" is where the counterexamples live.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-continuity-preimages.name: Continuity through preimages
ms-continuity-preimages.oneLine: f is continuous on all of X exactly when the preimage of every open set is open, and likewise for closed. It is the definition with the epsilons hidden, and it is what makes continuity a topological idea.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-bounded-linear-maps.name: Continuity of linear maps
ms-bounded-linear-maps.oneLine: For a linear map between normed spaces, continuous, continuous at zero and bounded are the same condition. Marked non-examinable in the notes.

ms-topological-spaces.name: Topological spaces
ms-topological-spaces.oneLine: Keep the rules about unions and intersections, drop the distance, and you have a topology. The notes offer this as a preview of where the course goes next rather than as examinable material.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-subspace-topology.name: Open sets of a subspace
ms-subspace-topology.oneLine: A subset of Y is open in Y exactly when it is the intersection of Y with something open in X. Being open stops being a property of a set and becomes a property of a set inside a named space.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-connectedness.name: Connectedness
ms-connectedness.oneLine: A space is disconnected when two disjoint nonempty open sets cover it. Connected is the negation, and the useful equivalent forms are "only the whole space and the empty set are both open and closed".

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-intervals-connected.name: The connected subsets of the line
ms-intervals-connected.oneLine: A nonempty subset of R is connected exactly when it is an interval. One classification, and every later statement about connected subsets of the line is read off it.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-connected-components.name: Connected components
ms-connected-components.oneLine: Each point lies in a largest connected set containing it, and those components partition the space. The sunflower lemma — connected sets sharing a point have connected union — is what makes the largest one exist.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-connectedness-continuity.name: Connectedness and continuous maps
ms-connectedness-continuity.oneLine: A continuous image of a connected space is connected. Applied to a real function on an interval that is the intermediate value theorem, and applied to the circle it gives the one-dimensional Borsuk–Ulam theorem.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-path-connectedness.name: Path connectedness
ms-path-connectedness.oneLine: Any two points joined by a continuous path. It implies connectedness and is strictly stronger: the topologist’s sine curve is connected because of one limit point and path connected to nothing across it.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-open-connected-path-connected.name: Open connected sets in a normed space
ms-open-connected-path-connected.oneLine: In a normed space, an open connected set is path connected — so the topologist’s sine curve can only exist because it is not open. Marked non-examinable in the notes.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-sequential-compactness.name: Sequential compactness
ms-sequential-compactness.oneLine: Every sequence has a subsequence converging inside the space. A sequentially compact space is complete, closed and bounded as a subspace, and closed subsets inherit the property.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-bolzano-weierstrass.name: Bolzano–Weierstrass in R^n
ms-bolzano-weierstrass.oneLine: Coordinatewise convergence plus a diagonal argument gives a convergent subsequence in every closed ball of R^n, and from there: a subset of R^n is sequentially compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.

ms-total-boundedness.name: Total boundedness
ms-total-boundedness.oneLine: For every epsilon, finitely many balls of that radius cover the set. Strictly stronger than bounded — the discrete line is bounded and not totally bounded — and equivalent to every sequence having a Cauchy subsequence.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-seqcompact-characterisation.name: Sequentially compact = complete + totally bounded
ms-seqcompact-characterisation.oneLine: The two halves of sequential compactness pulled apart: total boundedness produces a Cauchy subsequence, completeness makes it converge, and neither on its own is enough.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-compactness-continuity.name: Continuous maps on a compact space
ms-compactness-continuity.oneLine: A continuous image of a sequentially compact space is sequentially compact; a real-valued continuous function on one attains its bounds; and continuity on one is automatically uniform.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-equicontinuity.name: Uniform boundedness and equicontinuity
ms-equicontinuity.oneLine: Two conditions on a whole family of functions at once: one bound for all of them, and one delta that works for all of them at a point. Both are about the family, not about its members.

ms-arzela-ascoli.name: The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem
ms-arzela-ascoli.oneLine: A family of continuous functions on a sequentially compact space is totally bounded exactly when it is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous — so a closed such family is compact, and sequences in it have uniformly convergent subsequences.

ms-open-covers.name: Open covers and compactness
ms-open-covers.oneLine: A cover is a family of open sets whose union is the space; compact means every one of them has a finite subfamily that still covers. Showing a space is not compact means producing one bad cover.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-lebesgue-number.name: The Lebesgue number lemma
ms-lebesgue-number.oneLine: For a cover of a sequentially compact space there is a single radius such that every ball of that radius lies inside some one member. It is the step that turns subsequences into finite subcovers.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-compact-equals-seqcompact.name: In a metric space the two compactnesses agree
ms-compact-equals-seqcompact.oneLine: Compact, sequentially compact, and complete with totally bounded are the same condition for metric spaces — which is false for topological spaces in general, and is why the course can use whichever is convenient.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-heine-borel.name: The Heine–Borel theorem
ms-heine-borel.oneLine: A subset of R^n is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. The statement is about R^n and nothing else: in an infinite-dimensional normed space the closed unit ball is closed, bounded and not compact.

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

ms-dini-theorem.name: Dini’s theorem
ms-dini-theorem.oneLine: A monotone sequence of continuous functions on a compact space converging pointwise to a continuous limit converges uniformly. Drop compactness, monotonicity or continuity of the limit and it fails.

ms-baire-category.name: Urysohn, Tietze and Baire
ms-baire-category.oneLine: Separating closed sets by a continuous function, extending a continuous function off a closed set, the Cantor intersection property, and the Baire category theorem. All marked non-examinable in the notes.

readings.title: Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis
readings.where: Ch. 3, exercise 21 and Ch. 2 for Baire

readings.title: Sutherland, Introduction to Metric and Topological Spaces

p2-probability-axioms.name: The axioms, and why they need a sigma-algebra
p2-probability-axioms.oneLine: Non-negativity, total mass one and countable additivity over a sigma-algebra of events. The restriction to a sigma-algebra is not bureaucracy: not every subset of an uncountable space can be given a consistent probability.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-continuity-of-probability.name: Continuity of probability
p2-continuity-of-probability.oneLine: The probability of an increasing union is the limit of the probabilities, and likewise for a decreasing intersection. It is countable additivity rearranged, and it is how statements about "for ever" are made finite.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-union-bound.name: The union bound
p2-union-bound.oneLine: The probability that at least one of a list of events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities, with no independence assumed anywhere. Crude, free, and often all that is needed.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes
Alon & Spencer, The Probabilistic Method
readings.where: Ch. 1 — the union bound doing real work

p2-conditioning-independence.name: Conditioning, independence and random variables
p2-conditioning-independence.oneLine: Conditioning renormalises the measure onto an event; independence says conditioning changes nothing. A random variable is a measurable function on the sample space, which is what lets it be conditioned on.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-expectation.name: Expectation
p2-expectation.oneLine: Linearity holds with no independence at all, which is most of what expectation is for. For a non-negative integer variable the expectation is the sum of the tail probabilities, and sums of non-negative variables may be exchanged with expectation freely.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-strong-law.name: The strong law of large numbers
p2-strong-law.oneLine: For independent identically distributed terms with finite mean, the averages converge to the mean almost surely — one event of probability one, not a statement about each large n separately.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-convergence-notions.name: Almost sure against in probability
p2-convergence-notions.where: §1.6, the barred remarks, p. 11 (not required for the course)
p2-convergence-notions.oneLine: Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability and the converse fails. The notes set this out in a left-barred block, which marks it as outside the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §1.6, the barred remarks, p. 11 (not required for the course)

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-stochastic-processes.name: What a stochastic process is
p2-stochastic-processes.oneLine: A family of random variables indexed by time on one probability space. The index set being discrete or continuous is the first division in the course, and the questions are all about behaviour as time grows.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-random-walk.name: Simple random walk
p2-random-walk.oneLine: Partial sums of independent steps of plus or minus one. Return to the start only at even times and with probability given by a central binomial coefficient, which Stirling turns into an order of n to the minus a half.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-gamblers-ruin.name: Gambler’s ruin
p2-gamblers-ruin.oneLine: A walk between absorbing barriers at 0 and m. A one-step argument gives a linear difference equation whose solution is linear in k when the walk is fair and geometric in the odds ratio when it is not.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-game-duration.name: How long the game lasts
p2-game-duration.oneLine: The same one-step argument applied to the expected time to absorption. For the fair walk it is k(m − k), which is quadratic — a fair game between unequal purses ends quickly, between equal ones slowly.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-one-barrier.name: One barrier, and none
p2-one-barrier.oneLine: Letting the far barrier go to infinity: the walk with positive drift escapes with probability given by the odds ratio, and the fair walk hits every level with probability one while taking infinite expected time.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-stopping-times.name: Stopping times
p2-stopping-times.oneLine: A random time is a stopping time when whether it has arrived is decided by what has happened so far. "The first time the walk hits 5" is one; "the last time it is at 5" is not, and that is the whole distinction.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-wald-identity.name: Wald’s identity
p2-wald-identity.oneLine: The expected sum of a random number of independent identically distributed terms is the expected count times the expected term — provided the count is a stopping time with finite mean. Both conditions are load-bearing.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-markov-property.name: The Markov property
p2-markov-property.oneLine: Given the present, the future is independent of the past. Whether a process has it depends on what you call the state: a pair of consecutive steps can be Markov where their sum is not.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-n-step-transitions.name: Multi-step transitions
p2-n-step-transitions.oneLine: The n-step probabilities are the entries of the nth power of the transition matrix, and Chapman–Kolmogorov is matrix multiplication read as a sum over where the chain was in between.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-hitting-probabilities.name: Hitting probabilities and hitting times
p2-hitting-probabilities.oneLine: First-step analysis: condition on the first move and you get a linear system for the probability of ever reaching a set, and another for the expected time. The hitting probabilities are its minimal non-negative solution.

p2-hitting-minimality.name: Why the minimal solution is the right one
p2-hitting-minimality.where: §3.3, the barred proof, p. 31 (not required for the course)
p2-hitting-minimality.oneLine: The proof that the hitting probabilities are the least non-negative solution, by repeated substitution. The notes bar it out of the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §3.3, the barred proof, p. 31 (not required for the course)

p2-strong-markov.name: The strong Markov property
p2-strong-markov.oneLine: The Markov property holds at a stopping time, not only at a fixed time. It is what licenses "restart the chain when it first reaches i", and the proof of it is barred out of the course.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-recurrence-transience.name: Recurrence and transience
p2-recurrence-transience.oneLine: A state is recurrent when the chain returns to it with probability one, and then it returns infinitely often; transient otherwise, and then the sum of the return probabilities is finite. There is no third case.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-walks-in-dimensions.name: Random walks in d dimensions
p2-walks-in-dimensions.oneLine: Pólya’s theorem: the symmetric walk on the integer lattice is recurrent in one and two dimensions and transient in three or more. The proof sketch for d of three and above is barred out of the course.

p2-communicating-classes.name: Communicating classes
p2-communicating-classes.oneLine: Mutual reachability is an equivalence relation, so the state space splits into classes. Recurrence is a class property; every recurrent class is closed, and every finite closed class is recurrent.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-mean-return-times.name: Mean return times
p2-mean-return-times.oneLine: A recurrent state is positive recurrent when its expected return time is finite and null recurrent when it is not. Both are class properties, and the symmetric walk on the line is the standard null recurrent example.

p2-stationary-distributions.name: Stationary distributions
p2-stationary-distributions.oneLine: A distribution the chain leaves unchanged: a left eigenvector of the transition matrix for eigenvalue one, normalised. An irreducible chain has one exactly when it is positive recurrent, and then it is unique and equal to the reciprocal mean return times.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-periodicity-convergence.name: Periodicity and the convergence theorem
p2-periodicity-convergence.oneLine: The period of a state is the greatest common divisor of its possible return times, and it is a class property. Irreducible, aperiodic and positive recurrent is exactly when the distribution converges to the stationary one from any start.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-coupling.name: The coupling proof of convergence
p2-coupling.where: §3.12, the barred proofs and Theorem 3.60, pp. 45–49 (not required for the course)
p2-coupling.oneLine: Two copies of the chain run independently until they meet and then together; the one started stationary stays stationary, so the other converges. Beautiful, and barred out of the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §3.12, the barred proofs and Theorem 3.60, pp. 45–49 (not required for the course)

readings.title: Levin & Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times

p2-reversibility.name: Reversibility and detailed balance
p2-reversibility.oneLine: If a distribution satisfies the detailed balance equations it is stationary, and the chain run backwards looks the same. Birth–death chains and random walks on graphs are reversible, and detailed balance is far easier to solve than the full system.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-poisson-process.name: The Poisson process
p2-poisson-process.oneLine: Independent stationary increments with the count in an interval Poisson with mean rate times length. Two equivalent definitions: one by increments and one by the infinitesimal rate of a single arrival.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-poisson-derivation.name: Deriving the increment distribution
p2-poisson-derivation.where: §4.2, the barred derivation, pp. 55–56 (not required for the course)
p2-poisson-derivation.oneLine: Differential equations for the probability mass function, solved with a generating function and an integrating factor. The notes bar it out of the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §4.2, the barred derivation, pp. 55–56 (not required for the course)

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-arrival-times.name: Inter-arrival times and the memoryless property
p2-arrival-times.oneLine: The gaps between arrivals are independent exponentials of the same rate, and the exponential is the only continuous distribution that forgets how long it has already waited.

p2-superposition-thinning.name: Superposition and thinning
p2-superposition-thinning.oneLine: Two independent Poisson processes merge into one of the summed rate, and keeping each arrival independently with probability p splits one into two independent processes of rates p and 1 − p times the original.

p2-poisson-conditioning.name: Conditioning a Poisson process
p2-poisson-conditioning.oneLine: Given n arrivals by time t, they are distributed as the order statistics of n independent uniforms on the interval — the process has no preference about where they go. Exponential races fall out of the same algebra.

p2-inhomogeneous-poisson.name: Inhomogeneous and multidimensional Poisson processes
p2-inhomogeneous-poisson.oneLine: Let the rate vary with time, or drop time and scatter points in a region: the count in a set is Poisson with mean the integral of the rate over it, and disjoint sets stay independent.

readings.title: Kingman, Poisson Processes
readings.where: Ch. 2 — the general definition on a measure space

p2-ctmc-basics.name: Continuous-time Markov chains
p2-ctmc-basics.oneLine: A chain that waits an exponential time in each state and then jumps. The generator collects the jump rates, with each diagonal entry minus the sum of its row — the memoryless property is what keeps it Markov.

p2-jump-chain-explosion.name: The jump chain, and explosion
p2-jump-chain-explosion.oneLine: Separate where the chain goes from how long it waits: the jump chain is an ordinary discrete chain. If the holding times shrink fast enough the chain makes infinitely many jumps in finite time.

p2-ctmc-transition-probabilities.name: Transition probabilities and the Kolmogorov equations
p2-ctmc-transition-probabilities.oneLine: The transition matrices at each time satisfy Chapman–Kolmogorov and the forward and backward differential equations driven by the generator. The proofs, and the matrix exponential solution, are barred out of the course.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-ctmc-classification.name: Classifying the states of a chain in time
p2-ctmc-classification.oneLine: Irreducibility, recurrence and transience carry over, and are decided by the jump chain rather than by the rates — how long the chain waits does not change where it can get to.

p2-ctmc-stationary.name: Stationary distributions in continuous time
p2-ctmc-stationary.oneLine: The condition is pi times the generator equal to zero, not pi times a transition matrix. An irreducible chain is positive recurrent exactly when such a distribution exists, and then it is unique.

p2-queues.name: Queues
p2-queues.oneLine: Poisson arrivals and exponential service give a birth–death chain. The single-server queue is positive recurrent exactly when the arrival rate is below the service rate, and then its length is geometric in the ratio.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-conditional-expectation.name: Conditional expectation as a variable
p2-conditional-expectation.oneLine: The expectation of X given Y is a function of Y, and therefore itself a random variable. The tower property — its expectation is the expectation of X — is the identity every martingale argument runs on.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-martingales.name: Martingales
p2-martingales.oneLine: A process whose expected next value, given everything so far, is where it is now: a fair game. The symmetric walk, its square minus the time, and an exponential of it are the three standard examples.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-new-martingales.name: New martingales from old
p2-new-martingales.where: §6.2, Theorems 6.4–6.9 and Examples 6.5–6.10, pp. 80–82 (not required for the course)
p2-new-martingales.oneLine: Betting a predictable amount on a fair game keeps it fair — the discrete stochastic integral. The notes put this whole section outside the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §6.2, Theorems 6.4–6.9 and Examples 6.5–6.10, pp. 80–82 (not required for the course)

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-stopped-martingales.name: Stopped martingales
p2-stopped-martingales.oneLine: A martingale stopped at a stopping time is still a martingale, so its expectation at every finite time is still its starting value. The proof is barred out of the course; the statement is not.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-optional-stopping.name: Optional stopping, and what it computes
p2-optional-stopping.oneLine: Under a boundedness condition the expectation at the stopping time equals the starting value, which recovers the ruin probability and the game duration in two lines each. Drop the condition and the doubling strategy appears to make money.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-martingale-convergence.name: Martingale convergence
p2-martingale-convergence.where: §6.4, Theorem 6.18 and Example 6.19, pp. 85–86 (not required for the course)
p2-martingale-convergence.oneLine: A non-negative martingale converges almost surely, proved by an upcrossing argument; the Pólya urn is the example. The section is outside the course.

readings.title: Probability 2 — your lecture notes
readings.where: §6.4, Theorem 6.18 and Example 6.19, pp. 85–86 (not required for the course)

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-brownian-motion.name: Brownian motion
p2-brownian-motion.oneLine: Continuous paths, independent increments, and the increment over an interval normal with variance its length. The covariance of two times is the smaller of them, which is the whole of the dependence structure.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-brownian-symmetries.name: Symmetries of Brownian motion
p2-brownian-symmetries.oneLine: Negation, scaling time by a factor and space by its square root, time reversal on an interval, and inversion all give back a Brownian motion. Each one turns a hard question into an easier one.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-reflection-principle.name: The reflection principle
p2-reflection-principle.oneLine: Reflecting the path after it first hits a level gives another Brownian motion, so the running maximum has the same distribution as the absolute value, and the hitting time of a level gets a density in closed form.

readings.title: Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

p2-arcsine-laws.name: The arcsine laws
p2-arcsine-laws.where: §7.3, the barred remarks, pp. 94–96 (not required for the course)
p2-arcsine-laws.oneLine: Where the maximum falls, the last zero, and the time spent positive all have the arcsine distribution. The notes leave these as left-barred remarks outside the course.
